newsitem.title: ALBANIA: EU mission tells Tirana security comes before aid.
newsitem.headline: EU mission tells Tirana security comes before aid.

text.p: The head of a European mission to Albania said on Wednesday the authorities in the troubled Balkan country had to improve the security situation before outside help could be offered.

Dutch diplomat Jan de Marchant et d'Ansembourg, heading the 11-strong European Union team, said they had discussed humanitarian aid, financial issues and the security situation, adding that they considered the last to be the most important.
"Our aim is to get aid in as quickly as possible, and we will make a priority list of things that can be done right away," he told a news conference, adding that he could not go into detail.
"A number of things are dependent on the security situation, so we need to concentrate on that as a matter of priority."

Asked whether the European response to Albanian appeals for outside intervention to end the armed anarchy that has swept the country was a question of too little, too late, he replied: "I'm afraid that might be true of any help for Albania, but the problem is that Albania has to solve its own problems first."
"We are asking Albania to help us help them, they have to create a situation in the country so that the help we give them doesn't fall into the wrong hands," he said.
EU governments have already rejected Albanian demands for the deployment of a substantial international peace-keeping force to restore order.

Thousands of weapons are in private hands across Albania after the wholesale looting of weapons from army barracks, and the south is under the control of rebels seeking the removal of right-wing President Sali Berisha.

In a blunt assessment of the security situation in the country, he said: "The police are a shambles, there are no prisons, customs or border police and hardly any army, they need just about everything, I think you can imagine the sort of requests they made."
Despite this he believed Albanians had the means to restore normality in the country.
"I think they have more ability to do this than appears, I think they are making honest, serious efforts to get the country back to normal, and certain improvements can already be seen."
The team was due to fly to Italy on Wednesday at the end of its three-day fact-finding visit and will hand over a report to be presented to EU foreign ministers in Brussels on Monday.
